title: Textile traders and brokers
subtitle: Merchants who buy grey fabric, get it processed, and sell across India
covers: This page covers Surat textile traders (merchant-manufacturers and wholesalers) and the brokers who connect them. Traders coordinate the whole chain but usually own no looms or process houses.

snapshot.text: An ISID study (Mar 2026) describes traders as the coordinating agents of Surat's fragmented cluster, with small firm size used to spread risk and inventory.
Distributors across India often buy from Surat traders on 180 days' credit and sometimes return unsold goods after the credit period (FOSTTA, Jan 2026).
Fraud by buyers and brokers led to a proposed textile police station in the Salabatpura market area (Jun 2026).

items.text: Weavers sell grey fabric to merchants, who get it processed and sell it in Surat's markets (Textile Commissioner, old profile).
One 2026 industry source cites about 240 textile markets and over 70,000 traders in Surat; other counts differ.

items.text: Traders sit at both ends: they buy from weavers and send fabric to processors and embroiderers on job-work, then sell to wholesalers and retailers in other states.

blocks.note: General trading flow. Confirm with the customer.

Send to process house and embroidery units on job-work.
Finished goods held in market shops and godowns.

Collect payments; handle returns of unsold goods.

items.text: Overall finished fabric prices rose about 30% in 2026 according to a market representative, and outstation buyers in states such as Tamil Nadu and Karnataka resisted the new rates.
Ask for GST registration and returns, shop / establishment registration, market shop ownership or lease, and godown details. Trading needs no pollution consent.
Trader associations have started naming defaulting distributors on an app and in member groups; weaver associations publish lists of defaulting traders and brokers.

sections.title: Sales: who buys, how, and credit periods

items.text: Buyers are distributors, wholesalers and retailers across India; many order on 180 days' credit. FOSTTA discussed limiting credit to 70 days and returns to 30 days.
On the buying side, weavers say traders take 60-120 days or longer to pay them; weavers resolved in Sep 2026 to cap credit at 30 days.
Customer's debtor ageing, return rates and top outstation buyers: collect from the ledger and GST data.

blocks.text: No verified public margin or working-capital figure exists for Surat textile traders.

sections.title: Fragility points and early warning signs for a lender

items.text: Long receivables plus returns of unsold, out-of-fashion goods after six months.
Fraud by outstation buyers and brokers.
Cost pass-through limits: buyers in other states resisted 2026 price rises.
Thin capital: a trader may carry large stock and receivables on borrowed money and supplier credit.
Debtors beyond 180 days rising; frequent goods returns; weavers or processors complaining of delayed payment.
Cheque returns or frequent overdraws; cash credit used near the limit all month.
Electricity units falling month on month, or a shift stopped, without a matching fall in loan outstanding.
Creditor days stretching; suppliers charging late-payment interest; purchases switched to cash from new sources.
Stock or receivables building up; sales concentrated on one or two parties or brokers.
Wages paid late or labour leaving; regular weekly closures.
New borrowing from private lenders or related parties; machines rented out or sold.
